USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with the already-scheduled July 6 tariffs on ~$34B of Chinese imports as announced, but do not immediately trigger the threatened additional $200B tranche. Hold the current posture — let the scheduled tariffs land, gauge China's actual response, keep the negotiating channel open, and prepare relief mechanisms (e.g., CCC support to farmers) to contain the political blowback rather than escalating the size of the confrontation. This preserves US leverage and credibility while retaining room to de-escalate if Beijing blinks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate-positive (+0.3) rather than severe. The US holds the upper hand structurally: China's exports to the US are roughly four times US exports to China, and the US macro picture is healthy — the broad dollar is up ~3.4% to ~113.3, industrial production has risen to 103.4, and CPI at 251 remains moderate, so the dispute has not yet materially hit the real economy (country_health). But the downside risk is real and politically damaging: China has committed to matching retaliation effective July 6 targeting $14B of soybeans plus autos, aircraft and pork — squarely aimed at the farm belt ('soybeans are grown in states where Trump received strong support in 2016'), and soybean futures have hit one-year lows while markets tumbled with Boeing, Caterpillar and GM falling (timeline 6/15, 6/18; CNBC 7/2; NYT 6/19; farmpolicynews 6/17). This creates genuine pressure on a key domestic constituency ahead of the 2018 midterms, and firms are 'frozen in suspense' about whether tariffs are leverage or a permanent door (CSMonitor 6/29). An action stance of hold (0.0) fits: the scheduled tariffs are already locked and reversing now would forfeit credibility and leverage, but gratuitously escalating to the $200B tranche would worsen market/business confidence and invite wider retaliation. Maintaining the committed course while keeping negotiation open and shielding farmers is the coherent response to this level of threat.

US macro still healthy — dollar up ~3.4%, IP 103.4, moderate CPI; trade war not yet biting real economy (country_health)
US has structural leverage: China's exports to US ~4x US exports to China (NYT 6/19)

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with the already-announced, proportionate retaliation on July 6 as a matter of standing firm, but do not escalate beyond that level — keep dialogue channels open and avoid any new action that would hand Washington the pretext for the threatened $200B tranche. Hold our posture, signal willingness to return to the May 19 framework, and negotiate to cap the scope of the dispute and preserve the exports that can still be saved.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: This is a genuinely high-threat moment for China, not yet existential. The June 15 USTR final plan puts 25% tariffs on ~$34B (List 1, effective July 6) specifically targeting 'Made in China 2025' sectors (aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery, new materials), and June 18 directs a further 10%-on-$200B list conditioned on our retaliation — per USTR/enforcement analyses, if all tranches land, nearly 90% of US imports from China would be tariffed. Firm-level targeting is already demonstrated by the April 16 ZTE denial order; though a $1.7B deal to lift the ban was reached (June 7) and ZTE reshuffled its board June 29, it shows our reliance on US components is a strategic vulnerability. On the macro side, the US dollar index has strengthened toward ~113 and US 10Y yields rose through late June, consistent with dollar/financing pressure on the CNY, while the tariffs have not yet taken effect so no visible export damage has registered. Because China cannot match in-kind up to $450B, and because immediate escalation risks activating the far larger $200B tranche, the calibrated response is to hold retaliation at the mirroring $50B level already announced and actively negotiate rather than widen the conflict. An action_score of 0.0 (negotiate) fits a situation where the threat is high but the wisest move is de-escalation-by-negotiation, not concession (talks are not advanced enough for rollback) and not further escalation (which would make our position worse).
key_factors: US $50B Section 301 plan finalized June 15, List 1 ($34B) effective July 6 targeting Made in China 2025 sectors
June 18 threat of 10% tariffs on an additional $200B, conditioned on Chinese retaliation
ZTE denial order (April 16) and $1.7B settlement to lift ban, exposing US-component supply-chain dependence
May 19 joint statement / purchase framework collapsed by May 29; truce over
US dollar index strengthening toward ~113 and rising US yields pressuring CNY; tariffs not yet effective so no export damage yet
China cannot retaliate in-kind against potential $400-450B of tariffs
